name: FactorAlpha
short: An end-to-end quantitative stock recommendation platform: a data pipeline, a five-factor rating model, and the product API behind factoralpha.ai. Three tiers, 5,000+ US equities.
tags:
Python · FastAPI · Azure SQL
PostgreSQL · pandas · React
sub: A three-tier production system for rating US equities — cloud ETL into a warehouse, a multi-factor quant model, and an async product backend serving the live app.
role: Backend engineer across all three tiers — ingestion, modelling and the product API.
doc:
What it is

FactorAlpha is a stock recommendation product for US equities. Three systems make it work, and I build across all three: a cloud ETL platform that ingests fundamentals, prices and analyst estimates for 5,000+ tickers into a warehouse; a quantitative rating engine that scores roughly 2,900 stocks on five factors and grades them Strong Buy to Strong Sell; and an async product backend that serves ratings, fair-value analytics, portfolio tools and generated narratives to the app.

Architecture

Vendor market-data API→rate-limited ETL→SQL warehouse
→factor pipelines→dual scoring engines→IC-weighted composite
→ratings database→async product API→React app

Quarterly retrain, daily re-score. All three tiers run in production on Azure with automated scheduling, monitoring dashboards and run-report emails.

Tier one — the data platform

  • Rate limiting as a design constraint. The vendor allows a few hundred requests per minute across a quota that every process shares. I built a process-wide token-bucket limiter with deliberate headroom, feeding batched parallel per-ticker fetches. Nine schedulable job types cover prices, income statements, balance sheets, cash flow, ratios, key metrics, beta computation and analyst estimates.
  • Idempotency as the reliability model. Writes go through a staging table into a MERGE upsert keyed on ticker, fiscal year and period, with fill-when-empty semantics — numeric columns update only when null or zero, text only when null. Every re-run is safe, which means the nightly job and the gap-repair job are the same job. Recovery from a partial failure is "run it again".
  • Per-ticker fault isolation. Built after a real incident: one junk fiscal year overflowed a SQL integer and rolled back an entire batch. Now per-ticker database errors are caught, batch-mates are honestly downgraded, staging is recreated, and the run continues.
  • A survivorship-bias-free universe. Backfilled around 2,750 historical index members drawn from a decade of reconstitutions — roughly 2,000 of them delisted — across six tables using resumable standalone loaders.
  • WAN-optimised bulk loading. Per-row inserts were far too slow over a high-latency link, so writes became single-round-trip JSON batches exploded server-side, with a fast path for symbols seen for the first time.
  • Point-in-time analyst estimates. Estimates, price targets and grade consensus are ingested append-only and stamped with a retrieval timestamp on every run, so downstream features can be built without look-ahead bias.
  • Operations. A FastAPI job orchestrator with database-tracked job status and cron schedules, plus a React dashboard for run monitoring, log inspection and schedule management. Data-quality sanitisers handle the usual mess, including ticker normalisation across notation styles.

Tier two — the rating model

  • Five factors, 49 metrics — growth, profitability, valuation, risk and momentum — scored across roughly 2,900 stocks.
  • Two engines running side by side. A cross-sectional z-score model for large caps that uses point-in-time index membership, rolled forward from a constituent change-log so training panels contain the members as of that quarter. And a returns-calibrated bucket model for the rest of the universe, where each metric's direction is learned from mean realised forward twelve-month returns rather than pinned by theory — which also captures relationships that aren't monotonic.
  • IC-weighted composite. Factor weights are proportional to the absolute Spearman information coefficient against forward twelve-month returns, floored and capped between 10% and 30% with iterative redistribution, and re-estimated at every quarterly retrain. The composite maps to A–F sextiles, then to Strong Buy through Strong Sell.
  • Evidence-based choices, not folklore. Splitting risk into balance-sheet quality and price risk moved the walk-forward out-of-sample risk-adjusted spread from 0.28 to 0.40, using a provably weight-preserving recombination. The asset-growth anomaly was inverted on evidence. Momentum was pruned back to relative strength. Denominator guards route negative-earnings-style traps to "not meaningful" instead of silently producing nonsense.
  • Versioned cutover. Model versions switch atomically through a rating-type marker — old rows are retired, never deleted — so a bad release can be rolled back instantly.

Tier three — the product backend

  • Async FastAPI in a layered router → service → repository → ORM architecture: 19 routers, 20 service modules and 51 ORM models over a Postgres schema covering stocks, per-dimension rating tables, full financial statements, users, portfolios, watchlists, news, earnings and market data.
  • The product surface. Five-dimension and overall ratings; fair-value and intrinsic-value analytics with re-rate and IV anchors, entry and exit bands and upside-to-fair-value; screener, detail and comparison views; portfolio management with cost-basis tracking, rebalancing, health scores and Markowitz efficient-frontier optimisation; watchlists; analyst picks; market movers, indices and global markets; earnings calendar and transcripts.
  • LLM narratives. Generated explanations for stock comparisons, single-stock quant summaries, portfolio health checks and portfolio rating explanations — prompt-built from the platform's own factor scores and financials rather than the model's memory.
  • Ten scheduled jobs inside the application lifespan, pinned to US/Eastern: daily end-of-day prices and weekly quarterly financials synced from the trading warehouse, price history, earnings calendar, news on two cadences, fifteen-minute market data during trading hours, a daily index constituent refresh, and nightly fair-value and entry/exit band computation. Plus around 35 standalone seeder CLIs with dry-run support.
  • Engineering hygiene. Custom transactional and query decorators handling session injection and commit/rollback, Redis caching for live quotes and market data, JWT auth with password-reset flows, security-headers middleware, Alembic migrations, and multi-worker deployment behind the frontend.

The hard problems

  1. Survivorship bias, eliminated twice — once in the warehouse by backfilling delisted names, and once in the model by rolling index membership forward so it trains on members-as-of-quarter. Build a panel from today's index and every failed company is silently missing; the model quietly learns an optimistic history.
  2. Shared API-quota engineering — a process-wide token bucket with headroom by design, under a hard per-minute and per-month cap shared by every process on the platform.
  3. Three-source data reconciliation — vendor actuals, warehouse quarterlies and forecast-engine projections all write the same statement tables. I authored a per-column lineage document governing which source owns which value, and when actuals overwrite forecasts.
  4. External model validation — the model went through a formal two-way review with an independent quant team. I wrote the quantitative rebuttals and fixed the real defects it surfaced, including a risk-free-rate join bug and sector variants of the Altman-Z calculation.
  5. Look-ahead-bias-free features — point-in-time estimate snapshots and a unified forward-return convention across every factor.
  6. Production incident response across tiers — database contention timeouts, integer-overflow rollbacks, firewall onboarding, scheduler staggering to protect the source database, and silent-failure counters for rows scored without a risk-free rate.

The thread through all of it: in quant systems the expensive failures are silent. Nothing crashes when your training data is biased or your estimates leak the future — you just get confident, wrong ratings. Most of the engineering here is about making those failures loud.

name: FinSight
short: The complete backend for a US equities and options trading app — order execution against a live brokerage, options analytics, portfolio monitoring, and the GenAI assistant on top.
sub: The entire Python backend for an algorithmic trading platform — 87 REST endpoints across 9 domain modules, wired to a live brokerage, plus the retrieval-augmented assistant.
role: Backend engineer — orders, market data, analytics and monitoring; built the GenAI core; led the runtime migration.
note: Internal product — happy to walk through it on a call.
doc:
What it is

FinSight is an algorithmic trading application for US equities and options. This is its entire backend — the Python API layer sitting between the app, a live brokerage connection, a SQL database and several market-data providers. It covers the full lifecycle of a retail trading platform: user onboarding, market research, order placement, live monitoring and portfolio analytics, across 87 REST endpoints in nine domain modules. I also built the GenAI core.

Architecture

App→FastAPI (87 routes, 9 modules)→per-user brokerage gateway
↘SQL database↘market & news providers↘RAG assistant

Nine modules — user management, orders, market data, pricing, news, monitoring, container discovery, shared infrastructure and the API layer — all behind one uniform response envelope, so the client never has to special-case anything.

Orders — the core of the platform

  • The full lifecycle over the brokerage REST gateway: placement for both stocks and options including confirmation replies, modification, cancellation and exit — with both token-authenticated and service-to-service variants, the latter used by the automated trading engine.
  • Bracket-order management — profit-target and stop-loss modification, initial price capture, and unrealised-percentage tracking against those levels.
  • Status synchronisation. The broker is the source of truth for whether an order filled; the database is always a slightly stale opinion about it. Webhook-style status updates plus manual reconciliation keep the two honest.
  • Account and portfolio analytics — account summaries, latest portfolio value, portfolio time series for charting, top holdings, realised P&L, and exited, pending and cancelled trade lists for both options and stocks.
  • Contract resolution and session management — ticker to contract ID, strike to option contract ID, gateway auth-status checks, and per-user base-URL resolution, because every user gets their own gateway container.
  • Market open/close status and in-app order notifications with read/unread state.

Market data and options analytics

  • Historical and realtime data with UTC to IST and US timezone handling, candlestick chart data, price-change analytics and trading-day calculations.
  • The options engine — expiry dates, full option-chain retrieval, quotes, mid price, underlying price, Greeks, and a payoff calculator for visualising a strategy's profit and loss.
  • Open-interest analytics combining exchange data with a third-party options-chain API.
  • An async bulk fetcher for the end-of-day pipeline, using async HTTP with a semaphore-bounded concurrency pool and bulk database upserts, snapshotting the NASDAQ-100 universe keyed by pre-mapped contract IDs.
  • CSV-driven reference-data ingestion for the ticker master.

The GenAI core

  • A production retrieval-augmented conversational agent over vector and graph stores — Pinecone and ChromaDB for content, Neo4j for relationships between entities.
  • Rank-based retrieval and deliberate chunking, so retrieved context is re-ordered by relevance before it reaches the model rather than dumped in raw.
  • It lands around 90% response accuracy at low latency. The point is grounding: a general-purpose model has never seen this user's portfolio, and guessing is worse than useless in a trading context.

Everything else that had to work

  • Authentication — bcrypt password hashing, HS256 session tokens validated for signature, expiry and user existence on every protected route, plus stateless email OTP and temporary-password flows built on short-lived signed tokens carrying a retry counter.
  • Portfolio monitoring — mark-to-market revaluation of open positions, scheduled portfolio snapshots feeding historical graphs, and futures price snapshots for index display.
  • News and earnings intelligence — central-bank RSS ingestion, scraped equity news, an earnings calendar with pre- and post-earnings price-move analytics, and news filtered down to a user's actual holdings.
  • CI/CD — a multi-stage pipeline that builds, archives, publishes and deploys to Azure App Service on Linux.

The migration

The backend originally shipped as a serverless function app with 92 HTTP-triggered functions. It needed to become a normal web application. Rather than rewriting the business logic, I wrote an adapter that makes a FastAPI request object look exactly like the old function-style request, plus a file shim so CSV upload handling kept working unchanged.

The entire service layer carried over untouched. Every route was mounted under the same prefix, 39 typed request models were added on top with auto-generated API docs, and the frontend team never changed a line — zero modifications. Getting to keep the boring parts of a rewrite boring is underrated.

name: Rule AI
short: A no-code business rules engine for credit decisioning — analysts draw decision logic, chain it into workflow graphs, simulate it in bulk and publish it as a secured API. I built the backend.
sub: A no-code decision-management platform for lending and credit risk: visual rule authoring compiled into executable workflow graphs, bulk-simulated and published as production decision APIs.
role: Backend engineer — rule compiler, workflow DAG engine, bulk execution, caching, access control and governance.
note: Internal product — happy to walk through it on a call.
doc:
What it is

Rule AI is a no-code decision-management platform for lending and credit risk. Business users author decision rules visually, compose them into executable workflow graphs, test them against bulk datasets, and expose them as secure production decision APIs — without writing code. The backend is a FastAPI platform with 120+ REST endpoints powering loan approval, KYC and risk-scoring decisions.

Architecture

Visual authoring UI→rule compiler→workflow DAG engine
→Celery bulk execution→WebSocket progress→API-key decision endpoints

The compile-then-execute model

Every rule is stored in two representations: the authoring form exactly as the analyst drew it, which the UI loads back for editing, and an executable form compiled from it. Each rule type has a derive-from-UI and an evaluate function pair. Compilation also introspects the rule's input contract — which variables it depends on — and persists it alongside the rule, so the platform knows every rule's data requirements without anyone declaring them by hand.

Keeping the drawn version and the runnable version as separate representations of the same rule is what makes the system both editable and fast, instead of re-interpreting a UI tree on every single request.

Eight rule types

  1. Conditional — decision trees built from nested condition nodes with default branches.
  2. Dimensional — decision tables and two-dimensional grid lookups.
  3. Calculus — arithmetic formulas and chained calculation equations.
  4. Boundary and recommendation — credit-policy caps such as debt-service ratio, debt-to-income and loan amount, producing approve or decline recommendations.
  5. Code blocks — user-supplied Python, compiled with structured diagnostics that report syntax, indentation and import errors with line and column, stored in blob storage, hot-loaded through a module registry, and constrained to a curated allow-list of around twenty standard-library and approved scientific packages.
  6. Data fetchers — lookups against cached dataframes using generated pandas queries.
  7. API rules — outbound REST calls with JSON flattening, executed as a step inside a rule.
  8. Grid evaluation — matrix scoring variants.

The workflow engine

  • Rules chain into directed acyclic graphs of start, rule, recommendation and end nodes, with conditional edges and support for nested sub-workflows.
  • Outputs of upstream rules automatically publish as typed derived variables consumed downstream, so rules compose arbitrarily without manual wiring.
  • Execution is fully traced — per-node results and the traversal path — so the UI can highlight exactly which branch a decision took. That matters enormously when someone has to explain why an application was declined.
  • Graph validation, graded failure statuses, and final approve/decline decisioning.

Bulk execution — the problem that defined the project

Bulk simulation runs an entire dataset through a workflow before it goes live. It used to hold the request open and block the server.

  • Runs are now dispatched to Celery, which sizes a thread pool dynamically from live memory readings — a maximum usage fraction, a per-task memory budget and a worker cap — then chains a second task for bulk database persistence, decoupling compute from I/O.
  • The API answers immediately. Results are polled by task ID with computed test statistics, and progress streams back over WebSockets.
  • Clients cut workflow execution time by over 95%.

The fix wasn't a clever algorithm. It was accepting that a request should never wait for a long job — hand it to a worker, answer immediately, stream the truth as it arrives. That one change is where the 95% came from.

Three-layer caching

  • Redis write-through cache on every rule and workflow save, with whole-workflow warm and evict, plus rate limiting.
  • A Parquet-backed in-process dataframe registry, warmed at application startup for zero-latency data-fetcher lookups.
  • A disk cache with TTL for bulk test artifacts.
  • A nightly timezone-converted cron re-pulls every auto-refresh rule's data from source, rewrites the Parquet files and refreshes both the in-memory registry and Redis — with a file-lock guard so it can't execute twice across workers.

Governance and collaboration

  • A governed promotion lifecycle — rules are only editable while their workflow is in development; going live requires an approval request reviewed by an admin, with caps and email notification at every step. An auditable path from sandbox to production decisioning.
  • Externalised decision APIs — each live workflow gets a hashed API key stored column-deferred for security, and the platform auto-generates a ready-to-use request specification for the calling system.
  • Per-workflow role-based access control across six levels, with access-request flows.
  • Real-time presence over WebSockets, broadcasting who is editing a workflow, with stale-connection replacement.
  • Two-phase destructive operations — deleting a variable, category or data source first returns a full impact analysis of the affected rules and workflows in preview mode, requiring an explicit confirm call.
  • Full audit history of every create, update and delete with old and new values and the actor, plus soft deletes and versioned data archival with preview, restore and download.

The data layer

MySQL through SQLAlchemy 2.0 with Alembic migrations and connection pooling tuned for scale, plus a second independent engine connecting to the customer's system-of-record database for decision-time applicant lookups. Seventeen-plus tables across nine domains — rules, workflows, variables, tags, users, roles, data sources, upload groups and a generic audit-history table. JSON columns hold the rule and workflow representations, a pragmatic document-in-relational design that keeps the engine schema stable while rule structures keep evolving. Business users can register external MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, file and REST data sources, with variable metadata auto-derived from schema and dtype introspection.

name: corestrat.ai — backend + AI chatbot
short: Two production services behind the company website: the public chat backend API, and the retrieval-augmented GenAI engine that answers from Corestrat's own document corpus.
sub: Two production services live on corestrat.ai — a public FastAPI backend handling chat traffic, sessions and conversation persistence, and the RAG engine it delegates answers to.

metrics.k: of engine code authored by me

role: Principal author of the current RAG engine — pipeline, retrieval chain, production prompt, service layer, config and deployment. On the backend API: performance, background-task persistence, engine integration and a live database migration.
doc:
What it is

The chat system running on the company's public website, built as two separate production services. The first is the backend API the website talks to — it handles every incoming chat request, session and client metadata, and conversation persistence. The second is the GenAI engine it delegates to — a retrieval-augmented pipeline that answers strictly from Corestrat's own document corpus. I work on both: I'm the principal author of the engine as it runs today, and I did the performance and data-layer work on the backend.

Architecture

Website widget→Service 1 · chat backend API→Service 2 · RAG engine→Pinecone + OpenAI
↘MySQL conversation log (background task, off the response path)

Service one — the chat backend API

A FastAPI service exposed under a versioned path with a health endpoint, served by Uvicorn behind Gunicorn. It receives chat requests from the website widget, captures the session ID and forwarded client IP, persists the full conversation history to MySQL through SQLAlchemy, and delegates answer generation to the engine. The service was originally scaffolded by the wider team; the performance and data-layer work on it is mine:

  • Took database writes off the request path. Conversation logging was happening inside the request, so every visitor was waiting on a MySQL round-trip they didn't care about before seeing a reply. Moving persistence to background tasks removed that wait entirely.
  • Engine-integration parameter changes to keep the API and the rebuilt engine in lockstep through the transition.
  • A live database migration — connection and CA-certificate setup, ORM model changes, and a rework of the database manager, executed against a running service.

Service two — the RAG engine

Built on FastAPI, LangChain, OpenAI and Pinecone. It ingests the content corpus in PDF and DOCX form, chunks it with a recursive character splitter, embeds it into a Pinecone vector store, and answers through a RetrievalQA chain. The engine in production today is a rebuild I designed and wrote.

  • File-metadata caching on ingestion — unchanged documents are never reprocessed or re-embedded, which turns redeploys from slow into trivial.
  • The production prompt does the trust work. Grounded answers only, explicit rules for how products get listed, a graceful fallback for when the corpus genuinely has no answer, and a consistent assistant persona. A website assistant that invents product details is worse than no assistant at all.
  • An environment and config profile system, plus dependency management and deployment configuration, so the same codebase behaves correctly across environments.
  • A dedicated latency initiative ahead of the rebuild, tuning the response path of the live assistant.
  • Ongoing reliability work afterwards — memory maintenance, a Redis fix, session-ID handling, data-folder restructuring and import cleanup.

What I found interesting

Both wins here were latency, and neither came from the model. One sits in each service: on the engine, skipping re-embedding for unchanged files made deploys cheap; on the backend, moving conversation logging off the request path made responses fast. The clever part of a RAG system usually isn't the retrieval — it's everything you stop doing while the user is waiting.

A note on attribution

These are collaborative team repositories, so it's worth being precise. On the engine I'm the principal author of the codebase running in production — around 89% of surviving lines by git blame, and 42 of the repository's 78 commits, the largest individual contribution in the repo. On the backend API, the service was scaffolded by the wider team in late 2024 and my contributions are the 2025 performance and data-layer work described above. Every figure here is reproducible from the repository history.

name: RawDiary
short: A journaling app with no login at all. Usernames resolve in the browser against a Bloom filter in under 10ms — no database call to check if a name is taken. 100+ concurrent users at $0/month.
sub: A stateless, zero-authentication journaling app. No accounts, no identity database — and it runs at $0/month.
role: All of it — the Next.js frontend, the FastAPI backend, caching, spatial queries, audio masking and deployment.
doc:
The idea

Journaling apps ask you to make an account before you can write a sentence. I wanted the opposite: open it, pick a name, start writing, and have nothing about you stored anywhere.

How it works

Without accounts there's no users table, so checking whether a username is free can't be a database lookup. The server ships a Bloom filter to the browser — a probabilistic structure that answers "definitely free" or "possibly taken" in constant time. Availability resolves in under 10ms with no network round trip at all.

Feeds use cursor pagination cached in Redis rather than offset queries, so they stay fast as content grows rather than degrading with depth. Voice notes are pitch-shifted in the browser through the Web Audio API before upload, so the audio that leaves your device is already anonymous — the server never holds the original. Entries can be geotagged and queried spatially with PostGIS.

The innovation

Designing identity out of the system instead of protecting it. There's no auth to breach because there are no accounts, and the Bloom filter is what makes that practical rather than just idealistic. The whole thing runs on free tiers — 100+ concurrent users at $0/month — because there's so little to store.

What I built

All of it. The Next.js frontend and the client-side filter logic, the FastAPI backend, Redis caching, Supabase and PostGIS queries, the browser audio masking, and the deployment.

name: VeinChain
short: Logging in with the veins in your finger. We built the infrared capture hardware ourselves and put the identity record on Ethereum instead of in a database. Became two working apps and a paper.
sub: Finger-vein biometric authentication with enrolment anchored on-chain, built on custom low-cost infrared capture hardware.
role: Smart contracts, backend, frontends and the capture hardware.
doc:
The idea

Fingerprints and faces can be lifted from a photo or a glass. Vein patterns sit under the skin and only appear under near-infrared light, which makes them far harder to copy. The deeper problem is that biometric templates in a central database are a permanent liability — you can reset a password, you can't reset your hand.

How it works

An infrared capture rig images the finger, the vein pattern is extracted and processed into a template, and the identity record is committed to Ethereum through Solidity smart contracts rather than stored in a company database. Verification checks against the on-chain record, so there is no central store to breach and no administrator who can quietly alter enrolment history. A Flask service handles capture and matching; React and TypeScript frontends drive both applications.

The innovation

Two parts. Commercial vein scanners are expensive, so we built a low-cost capture rig ourselves — that's most of what made this a real project rather than a simulation. And putting enrolment on-chain makes the audit trail of who registered and when tamper-evident by construction rather than by policy.

What shipped

Two standalone applications — a web biometric login system and a blockchain-backed attendance tracker — along with a written paper documenting the approach.

name: RAG-app
short: Ask questions about your own PDFs without anything leaving your laptop. LangChain pipeline running Llama 3 locally — zero API cost, and documents never travel.
sub: Retrieval-augmented question answering over your own documents, running entirely on your machine.
doc:
The idea

Most document-chat tools send your files to somebody else's servers. For anything sensitive — contracts, medical records, internal documents — that's a non-starter, and the API bill grows with every question asked.

How it works

Documents are split into chunks, embedded into a local vector store, and the relevant chunks are retrieved and passed as context to a Llama 3 model running on the same machine. Scanned PDFs go through OCR first, so image-only documents work too. FastAPI serves the pipeline with documented endpoints; Streamlit gives it an interface you can actually use.

The innovation

Nothing about the architecture is exotic — the point is where it runs. Everything is local, so the cost per question is zero and no document ever leaves the host. It's the version of this tool you can point at files you're not allowed to upload.

name: EDU-AI
short: A learning platform that works out how you learn. A short survey infers VARK and MBTI style, a Random Forest classifier predicts it at 91% accuracy, and the material adapts to match.
sub: A personalised learning platform that infers how a student learns and reshapes the material to match.
role: Full stack — the Flask backend and MySQL data layer, the Random Forest classifier, the Gemini content generation and the interface.
doc:
The idea

Two students can sit through the same lecture and take away completely different amounts, largely because the format suits one of them and not the other. If a platform can work out how someone prefers to take in information, it can reshape the same material to fit.

How it works

A first-login survey captures signals mapped to two frameworks — VARK for sensory learning preference and MBTI for personality type. A Random Forest classifier predicts the learner's style from those responses at 91% accuracy. The prediction then drives content generation through the Gemini API, so the same topic is delivered as a diagram, a walkthrough or a written explanation depending on who's asking.

What I built

The full stack of it — the Flask application and MySQL data layer, the survey and scoring logic, the classifier and its training, the Gemini integration for adaptive content, and the interface students actually use.

The innovation

Combining two different models of the learner rather than one. VARK alone tells you the format; personality type shapes pacing and framing. Feeding both into the classifier is what got accuracy to 91%, and using an LLM at the delivery end meant not having to hand-author every variant of every lesson.
